flashcards.q: What is a micro-partition and what per-column metadata does it carry?
flashcards.a: An immutable, contiguous storage unit holding 50-500MB of uncompressed data (~16MB compressed), created automatically. Each carries per-column min, max, null count, and distinct count metadata used for pruning.

flashcards.q: How does pruning work and does it require an index?
flashcards.a: A query's WHERE predicate is checked against each micro-partition's min/max metadata before scanning any actual data; partitions that can't match are skipped entirely. No user-managed index is involved - pruning effectiveness depends on physical row ordering, which clustering keys control.

flashcards.q: Scale up vs scale out - how do you decide which fixes a performance problem?
flashcards.a: Scale up (bigger warehouse) fixes one slow query that's spilling to disk/remote storage (memory-constrained). Scale out (multi-cluster) fixes queueing from many concurrent queries competing for one warehouse. Sizing up for a concurrency problem wastes money; multi-cluster does nothing for one slow query.

flashcards.q: Warehouse T-shirt sizing and recommended auto-suspend defaults?
flashcards.a: Each size doubles credits/hour: XS=1 up to 6XL=512. Auto-suspend recommended ~60s for interactive/BI warehouses, ~30s for programmatic ETL - a suspended warehouse burns zero credits.

flashcards.q: Name the three caching layers and what's lost when a warehouse suspends.
flashcards.a: Result cache (account-wide, ~24h, exact-SQL-text-keyed, zero compute on hit), local disk/warehouse cache (recently-scanned micro-partitions on SSD, LOST entirely on suspend), and remote storage (durable, always correct, slowest).

flashcards.q: Time Travel retention by edition, and Fail-safe's role?
flashcards.a: Standard Edition: 1 day default/cap. Enterprise+: extendable up to 90 days. Fail-safe is a fixed, non-configurable 7-day window after Time Travel expires, recoverable only via Snowflake support - not self-service. Max total protection: up to 97 days.

flashcards.q: How does zero-copy clone avoid the storage cost of copying a 50TB table?
flashcards.a: The clone points at the same underlying immutable micro-partitions as the source - nothing is physically copied. Storage cost only appears for newly-written micro-partitions once the clone or source diverges. The clone gets its own independent retention clock going forward.

flashcards.q: What are the three stream types and what do they track?
flashcards.a: Standard (full CDC: inserts/updates/deletes), append-only (inserts only, cheaper, fits event/log sources), and insert-only (for external tables). A stream records an offset; querying it returns the delta since the offset was last consumed.

flashcards.q: Why guard a task with SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA?
flashcards.a: Without it, a scheduled task burns a full warehouse resume/query cycle on every interval regardless of whether the stream has any new data to process - real, avoidable credit cost from a missing guard clause.

flashcards.q: What does spilling to remote storage in a query profile indicate, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: An operator (sort, hash join, aggregation) needed more memory than local disk could provide and spilled all the way to cloud storage - the slowest tier. Signal the warehouse is undersized for that query's working set; fix by scaling up, not by adding a clustering key (clustering affects scanning, not in-memory processing).

flashcards.q: When is a clustering key worth the automatic-clustering cost, and when is it wasted?
flashcards.a: Worth it: large table (multi-TB+), queries consistently filter on that column, natural insertion order doesn't already serve it. Wasted: small table, unpredictable filter patterns, or natural load order already aligns with queries (most time-series tables need no explicit key).

flashcards.q: Snowflake per-credit pricing by edition (AWS US East, on-demand)?
flashcards.a: Standard ~$2/credit, Enterprise ~$3/credit, Business Critical ~$4/credit. Capacity contracts reduce these rates 20-45% depending on volume/term.

flashcards.q: When is Snowflake usually the wrong platform choice?
flashcards.a: Heavy ML/feature-engineering or large-scale unstructured-data pipelines (Snowpark narrows but doesn't close the gap to a real ML platform), or a single small, predictable workload that doesn't need elastic multi-cluster concurrency.
